extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and illustrators studying depiction of trees and foliage
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for representing trees and foliage truthfully in landscape painting, including rules for stems, branches, leaf-massing, light, and atmospheric treatment. Emphasises natural structure and visual effects that distinguish competent from false representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of vegetation / fidelity in foliage
rubrics_metrics.description: If the old masters do not give us truth here, they cannot have the faculty of truth in them; foliage is the chief component part of pictures and must be finished with care and labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foliage is the principal subject for landscape painters; faithful representation of vegetation is a primary test of an artist's truthfulness. Demonstrate this by close observation and exact rendering of the structural and optical properties of trees and leafage. Examples of failures (Claude, Gaspar Poussin) and successes (Turner, J. D. Harding) illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches do not taper; they divide
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the stems nor the boughs of ordinary forest trees taper, except where they fork: wherever a stem sends off a branch the parent stem is instantly less in diameter by the exact quantity of the branch and then remains of the same diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not draw smooth, continuous tapering of branches except where explained by forks. Represent diminution as stepwise at ramification points. The text gives the law as imperative and without exception for European forest trees (oak, elm, ash, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent tapering must be explained by lost sprays and ramification
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight appearance of tapering is caused by frequent buds and the dropping off of twigs which leave excrescences; where there is no real fork or past ramification, tapering is scarcely detectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you represent slight tapering, show the vestiges of past ramification (stumps, excrescences) or spray insertion. Avoid inventing smooth taper without anatomical cause; account for any diminution by the history of shoots and lost twigs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on continuous smooth tapering (quantitative rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: No bough ever, with appearance of smooth tapering, loses more than one tenth of its diameter in a length of ten diameters; any greater diminution must be accounted for by visible ramification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this numeric guide when inventing or simplifying forms: continuous taper greater than ~10% per ten diameters is implausible and should instead be rendered as a series of forks/steps. This is used to detect carrot-like, parsnip stems (Gaspar Poussin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches must diminish where they divide (conservation at forks)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible that the smallest shoot can be sent out of a bough without a diminution of the diameter above it, and wherever a branch goes off it must not only be less in diameter than the bough from which it springs, but the bough beyond the fork must be less by precisely the quantity of the branch it has sent off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing branch structures, ensure the parent limb's diameter is reduced by the material sent into child branches. Violations (branches equal to or thicker than parent) are a sign of false construction in old masters' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boughs must multiply as they diminish; outer spray bulk approximates trunk
rubrics_metrics.description: As branches divide they increase in number in precise proportion to their diminution of size, so that the outer sprays, if united, would generally just make up the diameter of the trunk (precision not strictly required, but the eye expects comparable bulk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render increasing multiplicity toward extremities: many slender twigs and sprays forming an intricate mass. Avoid drawings where each limb only forks two or three times and then vanishes without the expected complexity. Guidance includes the two-equal-ramification approximate ratios (each about two-thirds diameter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express complexity of outer sprays by massed, involved strokes and aerial gradation
rubrics_metrics.description: At the extremities the sprays form a mass of intricacy scarcely distinguishable from fine herbage and beyond power of definite representation; it can only be expressed by a mass of involved strokes with gradations of aerial perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt leaf-by-leaf depiction at the limits of visibility; instead use varied strokes, densities, and aerial perspective to suggest depth and intricacy. Show some sprays distinct and others faint to convey distance and interpenetration of branches and leaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornamental, patterned leaf-groups and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural leafage is not a repeated, identical bunch pattern; the perpetual repetition of the same shape and the same arrangement is like ornamental patterning and is false (Gaspar Poussin's circular, repeated groups are criticised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce irregularity: differing leaf orientations, foreshortenings, crossings, and accidental forms. Refrain from laying identical circular groups (scales) across a mass of foliage; variety at micro- and macro-scale is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve transparency, crumbling lights, and internal interstices in foliage
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves when massed are never opaque; they are transparent with crumbling lights letting one see through to the sky, producing masses of illumined foliage and deep passages of broken, irregular gloom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render foliage so that light slips through in patches and punctures: include sparkling lights, internal reflections, and chiaroscuro within the mass. Avoid flat, opaque brown masses without interstices (Gaspar Poussin example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unity, vaporescence, and repose in leaf masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature secures an exceeding harmony and repose in foliage: minute parts blend into a cloud-like harmony of shade, producing a flat, misty, unison of tone which keeps the eye in repose amid profusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance intricacy with overall unity: ensure distant or shadowed foliage reads as a quiet plane or veil. Over-emphasis on detail can destroy this unity (Both, Hobbima failures). Use tonal gradations to create restful passages against which form can be revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify distant foliage into masses; avoid leaf-by-leaf rendering at distance
rubrics_metrics.description: In middle distances and distance it is impossible that leaves be separately seen; painters who work leaf by leaf lose the truth of mass, producing dots and touches expressive of improbably large leaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In middle and far distances, suggest foliage by masses, tonal shapes, and softened edges rather than discrete leaf shapes. Reserve leaf detailing for near foreground where individual leaves can be resolved (Turner and Creswick examples juxtaposed with Both/Hobbima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches and boughs keep their angles even in wind; do not draw elastic, angleless limbs
rubrics_metrics.description: The fiercest wind cannot take the angles out of the bough of a tree an inch thick; the whole bough bends retaining its elbows and angles—angles are not destroyed by wind but result in curvature of parts around existing joints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting wind-affected trees, bend segments while keeping joint angles evident; avoid drawing limbs as smooth, India-rubber curves—that creates weakness not strength in the composition (Gaspar Poussin's storm trees criticised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Render woody stiffness, growth-lines and bark texture (distinct from animal curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a peculiar stiffness and spring about the curves of the wood which separates them from animal curves; bark is significant—wrinkles round the trunk, longitudinal bursting, indications of growth and age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study wood fibre and bark: indicate muscular woody lines, growth swells, wrinkles around arm-places, peeling or bursting where appropriate. Avoid flaccidity and animal-like sinuosity; forest study yields subtleties escapeable by figure-studied artists alone. Use the right fine lines to imply woody character (Titian and Turner praised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal outlines of tree masses often form symmetrical curves
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a universal termination of trees in symmetrical curves (a principle noted as important though often unobserved by old masters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing the silhouette of a tree or group, consider the overall curved termination shapes—symmetry and rounded massing help render convincing tree outlines. Use these in contrast to overly ragged or patterned rims.
